articles.title: After fight with husband at temple, woman sets herself, 2 sons ablaze in Tamil Nadu
articles.summary: Madurai: A 28-year-old woman and her two sons, 5 and 3, died after she allegedly set herself and the children on fire following a family dispute in Tenkasi.
articles.body: Madurai: A 28-year-old woman and her two young sons died after she allegedly set herself and the children on fire following a family dispute near Sivagiri in Tenkasi district on Monday.The deceased were Mariammal of Vadakkuchathiram West Street, and her sons Kabineshwaran, 5, and Rabineshwaran, 3. Mariammal was married to Kalipandi, 30, a painter, for six years. Kabineshwaran was a Class I student at a govt school, while Rabineshwaran attended an anganwadi centre.Police said Kalipandi was addicted to alcohol and frequently quarreled with his wife. The incident occurred after Mariammal took her children to a temple festival at Vadakkuchathiram. She also participated in a kummi dance with other women there. Kalipandi arrived at the temple under the influence of alcohol and created a ruckus with her. An upset Mariammal returned home with the children.Police said Mariammal allegedly locked the house from inside, poured kerosene on herself and the children, and set them on fire. Hearing their cries, neighbours rushed to the house, broke open a portion of the roof and extinguished the flames.Mariammal died at the spot, while her two sons, who sustained severe burns, were initially taken to Tenkasi Govt Hospital, and later shifted to Palayamkottai GH for advanced treatment. However, both children succumbed to their injuries one after another on Tuesday. Bodies were sent to the govt hospital for postmortem examination. articles.title: Acidente em Pontal, SP: identificados mãe e filho mortos em colisão | G1
articles.standfirst: Batida entre dois carros aconteceu na estrada vicinal Plínio Castro Prado na quarta-feira (7). Vítimas foram enterradas no cemitério municipal.
articles.summary: O grave acidente vitimou Leonídia e Leandro Huesca na estrada Plínio Castro Prado, deixando também feridos em estado grave após colisão frontal entre dois carros.
articles.body:
Leandro Eduardo Huesca e a mãe, Leonídia dos Santos Huesca, mortos em colisão em rodovia entre Pontal (SP) e Cândia — Foto: Redes sociais

Os corpos de mãe e filho mortos na colisão na estrada vicinal Plínio Castro Prado entre Pontal (SP) e o distrito de Cândia foram enterrados na tarde desta quinta-feira (8).

Leonídia dos Santos Huesca, de 63 anos, e Leandro Eduardo Huesca, de 35 anos, foram sepultados no Cemitério Municipal de Pontal . Eles morreram na última quarta-feira (7). O Ford Focus em que eles estavam bateu de frente com um Toyota Corolla.

Segundo o boletim de ocorrência, o motorista do Corolla, Fabio Santos da Silva, voltava da usina onde trabalha. Ele tinha ido apresentar a documentação para cumprir uma licença paternidade.

A família seguia de Pontal para Cândia. Leonídia e Leandro morreram na hora. No carro deles também estava a cunhada de Leandro, Bruna dos Santos.

Ela foi socorrida em estado grave e encaminhada à Unidade de Emergência do Hospital das Clínicas (HC-UE), em Ribeirão Preto (SP), onde permanece internada.

Segundo o médico Edmilson Guedes Nunes, do Grupo de Resgate e Atenção às Urgências e Emergências (Grau), Bruna teve traumatismo cranioencefálico e precisou ser intubada.

Fabio foi levado a um hospital particular em Sertãozinho (SP), também com vários ferimentos graves.

O trecho onde aconteceu o acidente é de pista simples e a ultrapassagem é proibida.

A perícia esteve no local e deve apontar as causas da colisão.

Nas redes sociais, a Prefeitura de Pontal manifestou pesar pelas mortes de mãe e filho e pelos feridos.

Colisão entre carros causa mortes em rodovia entre Pontal e o distrito de Cândia, no interior de SP — Foto: Alexandre David/EPTV

Vídeos: Tudo sobre Ribeirão Preto, Franca e região

articles.title: Mulher de 63 anos morre ao tentar atravessar a RJ-106 em Maricá | G1
articles.standfirst: Acidente aconteceu no km 28, em Itapeba, na noite desta quarta-feira (8). Um mês atrás, outra pessoa morreu no local.
articles.summary: Acidente aconteceu no km 28, em Itapeba, na noite desta quarta-feira (7). Um mês atrás, outra pessoa morreu no local.
articles.body:
Idosa morre atropelada em Maricá no início da noite de quarta-feira (8) — Foto: Adriano Marçal

Uma mulher de 63 anos morreu após ser atropelada por uma caminhonete por volta das 18h desta quarta-feira (7), na RJ-106, em Itapeba, Maricá , na Região Metropolitana do Rio. A vítima tentava atravessar a rodovia na altura do km 28. Segundo o Corpo de Bombeiros, ela morreu no local.

O atropelamento acontece exatamente um mês depois de outro caso semelhante no mesmo trecho da RJ-106, quando uma pessoa morreu na altura de Itapeba, por volta do mesmo horário.

Duas pessoas que estavam na caminhonete também ficaram feridas. Um homem de 60 anos e uma mulher de 36 foram socorridos e levados para o Hospital Municipal Dr. Ernesto Che Guevara, em Maricá. A prefeitura informou que foram atendidos e receberam alta.

A RJ-106 atravessa áreas urbanizadas de Maricá, com casas e estabelecimentos comerciais às margens da pista. Com isso, há circulação de pedestres que precisam atravessar a rodovia para chegar a outros pontos da cidade. À noite, a iluminação em alguns trechos pode dificultar a visualização de quem está às margens da estrada.

A Prefeitura de Maricá informou que realiza estudos e avalia a viabilidade de implantação de iluminação por energia solar nos trechos que ainda não possuem rede de baixa tensão. Nos que possuem, segundo a administração, a iluminação pública já está implantada e recebe manutenção periódica.

Outra situação que coloca em risco os pedestres é o costume de atravessar a pista fora das passarelas. Alguns pedestres justificam a prática alegando que é grande a distância entre as passarelas.

Segundo a Prefeitura de Maricá, o município já construiu dez passarelas ao longo da RJ-106 nos últimos anos. Uma delas, inclusive, fica em Itapeba. Ainda de acordo com a Prefeitura, outras três passarelas estão em construção: uma no km 21, em São José, outra no Condado e uma terceira no km 24, em Ponta Grossa, que está em estágio mais avançado.

A Prefeitura informou que as passarelas são custeadas e construídas pelo município, com acompanhamento e autorização do Departamento de Estradas de Rodagem do Estado do Rio de Janeiro (DER-RJ).

O órgão informou que as rodovias RJ-106 e RJ-104 vêm recebendo blitzes educativas nos trechos com maiores índices de acidentes. Segundo o DER, as ações têm o objetivo de conscientizar motoristas e pedestres sobre o respeito à sinalização, os riscos de comportamentos imprudentes e a importância de atitudes seguras no trânsito.

A previsão, segundo o departamento, é ampliar essas ações para outras regiões do estado até o fim do ano.

O DER-RJ informou que vai realizar, na próxima segunda-feira (12), novos serviços de reparo no pavimento da RJ-106, dando continuidade às ações de manutenção e melhoria das condições de circulação e segurança da rodovia.

O DER informou ainda que está conduzindo uma nova licitação para ampliar os serviços de conservação em toda a malha rodoviária estadual. A contratação prevê reparos no pavimento, renovação da sinalização horizontal e vertical, roçada, limpeza dos sistemas de drenagem e outros serviços de manutenção.
tags: Departamento de Estradas de Rodagem do Estado

articles.title: Morre idosa que foi atropelada por ônibus em Resende | G1
articles.standfirst: Acidente aconteceu nesta quinta-feira (8), na Rua Sebastião José Rodrigues, no bairro Campos Elíseos.
articles.summary: Acidente aconteceu nesta quinta-feira (8), na Rua Sebastião José Rodrigues, no bairro Campos Elíseos.
articles.body:
Hospital de Emergência de Resende — Foto: Divulgação/TV Rio Sul

Uma idosa, de aproximadamente 70 anos, morreu nesta quinta-feira (8), no Hospital de Emergências de Resende (RJ), após ter sido atropelada por um ônibus.

O atropelamento aconteceu na Rua Sebastião José Rodrigues, no bairro Campos Elíseos, por volta de 9h20. A vítima foi encaminhada para a unidade médica com ferimentos graves.

De acordo com o Hospital de Emergências de Resende, a idosa não resistiu aos ferimentos e morreu.

A identidade da idosa e as circunstâncias do acidente não foram divulgadas.

articles.title: Morre idoso que ficou ferido em explosão em rodoviária | G1
articles.standfirst: Vítima de 86 anos estava internado em estado grave no Hugol após ser atingido no dia 30 de setembro. Causa do acidente na rodoviária de São Simão ainda é investigada pelas autoridades.
articles.summary: João Melo Lima morreu no Hugol após ser atingido pela explosão na rodoviária de São Simão, que deixou o idoso com 63% do corpo queimado.
articles.body:
Morreu nesta quinta-feira (8) o idoso João Melo Lima, de 86 anos, que ficou ferido na explosão que aconteceu na rodoviária de São Simão , no sul do estado. Segundo o Corpo de Bombeiros, a vítima teve queimaduras em 63% do corpo. João estava internado no Hospital Estadual de Urgências Governador Otávio Lage de Siqueira (Hugol), em Goiânia .

De acordo com a apuração da TV Anhanguera, João Melo ficou nove dias internado na Unidade de Tratamento Intensivo (UTI) do Hugol e, até o último boletim, ele estava sedado e respirando com a ajuda de aparelhos. A morte foi confirmada pelo hospital durante a tarde.

João Melo Lima, de 86 anos, estava internado no Hugol — Foto: Reprodução/TV Anhanguera

Em um vídeo exibido pela TV Anhanguera, uma testemunha contou que estava passando por perto no momento da explosão, que quase atingiu o carro dela. Nas imagens, é possível ver um homem sentado ao fundo, no meio dos escombros (veja acima) .

O idoso João Melo foi atingido por uma explosão que aconteceu na rodoviária de São Simão na madrugada do dia 30 de setembro, quando ele chegava para trabalhar em uma lanchonete. Segundo os bombeiros, aconteceu uma explosão de maior intensidade, seguida de outras duas de menor proporção na área de boxes da rodoviária.

Durante a avaliação inicial, a equipe do Corpo de Bombeiros disse que identificou três botijões de cozinha e um sistema de gás canalizado na edificação. O laudo da polícia científica que vai determinar o que causou a explosão na rodoviária ainda não ficou pronto.

Ainda segundo a TV, João Melo era natural do Ceará e morava em Goiás há mais de 50 anos. Ele deixou 21 filhos, além dos netos e bisnetos. A família disse que o velório e o sepultamento vão acontecer na cidade de São Simão, mas a data e o horário ainda não foram divulgados.

articles.title: Hospital do Câncer de Nova Friburgo tem nova previsão para novembro | G1
articles.standfirst: Hospital está em fase final de acabamento e instalação de equipamentos; previsão de entrega é 28 de novembro, mas prazo pode se estender até o fim do ano.
articles.summary: Hospital está em fase final de acabamento e instalação de equipamentos; previsão de entrega é 28 de novembro, mas prazo pode se estender até o fim do ano.
articles.body:
Hospital do Câncer de Nova Friburgo deve ser entregue em novembro. — Foto: Pablo Pais/g1

A Prefeitura de Nova Friburgo , na Região Serrana do Rio, anunciou uma nova previsão para a inauguração do Hospital Estadual de Oncologia Francisco Faria.

Segundo o prefeito Johnny Maycon, após reunião com o secretário estadual de Saúde, Ronaldo Damião, a unidade deverá ser entregue em 28 de novembro. O prazo, porém, pode se estender até o fim do ano.

De acordo com a Secretaria Estadual de Saúde e a Fundação Saúde, o hospital está em fase final de acabamento, com os equipamentos de imagem sendo instalados, e deverá iniciar em breve o processo seletivo para a contratação dos profissionais.

A expectativa é que o hospital atenda pacientes adultos com câncer de Nova Friburgo e de outros municípios da Região Serrana. A estrutura contará com 48 leitos de enfermaria, dez leitos de terapia intensiva (UTI) e cinco salas cirúrgicas.

Também estão previstos serviços de radioterapia, quimioterapia, oncologia clínica, cirurgia oncológica, cuidados paliativos, reabilitação e diagnóstico. O centro de imagem terá equipamentos de ressonância magnética, tomografia, mamografia, raio X e ultrassonografia.

A unidade é aguardada há mais de uma década e acumula sucessivas mudanças no cronograma desde que foi anunciada pelo Governo do Estado, em 2012.

A proposta de criação do hospital surgiu em 2012, quando o Governo do Estado anunciou a implantação de uma unidade oncológica no prédio do antigo Centro Adventista de Vida Saudável (Cavs), no bairro Ponte da Saudade.

A primeira previsão de inauguração era para 2014, mas o prazo não foi cumprido. Depois disso, novas datas foram divulgadas, incluindo 2016, junho de 2023, janeiro de 2024, o fim de 2024 e o primeiro trimestre de 2025, sem que a unidade entrasse em funcionamento.

As obras chegaram a ser interrompidas e foram retomadas definitivamente em junho de 2022, após a reformulação do projeto. Na época, o investimento previsto era de cerca de R$ 51 milhões, com prazo de 12 meses para conclusão.

Em junho de 2025, o Estado realizou uma cerimônia para marcar a conclusão das obras estruturais. A etapa seguinte previa a instalação dos equipamentos e a preparação da unidade para receber pacientes.

O investimento previsto para o hospital também foi alterado diversas vezes ao longo da execução do projeto.

Em 2014, o valor estimado era superior a R$ 48 milhões. Com a retomada das obras, em 2022, o contrato passou para cerca de R$ 51 milhões. Em 2024, o investimento divulgado era de R$ 65,3 milhões, além de quase R$ 10 milhões destinados a adaptações posteriores.

Já em 2025, o valor anunciado chegou a cerca de R$ 75 milhões. Em março de 2026, a Secretaria Estadual de Saúde informou que o investimento total previsto para a unidade ultrapassava esse valor.

Em julho deste ano, a pasta divulgou uma nova previsão de entrega para outubro de 2026. À época, o adiamento foi justificado pela necessidade de ajustes finais, incluindo serviços de acabamento e a instalação do sistema de ar-condicionado nas áreas de tomografia e ressonância.

articles.title: HC stays parking fee collection at Khammam Govt Hospital
articles.summary: Telangana High Court stays parking fee collection from patients and attendants at Khammam Govt District Hospital; counters sought, next hearing Nov 12.
articles.body: Hyderabad: Telangana high court on Thursday ordered an interim stay on collection of parking fee from patients and their attendants at Govt District Hospital, Khammam.Hearing a petition challenging parking fee collection at the health facility, Justice B Vijaysen Reddy ordered counters be filed by municipal administration and urban development department, director of medical education, Khammam collector and the hospital superintendent, while adjourning the case to Nov 12 for further hearing.The judge passed the directions while hearing a petition filed by Timmana Naveen Raju and Wazeed Mohmmad of Khammam town. Their counsel Ambedkar Dunna argued that authorities at the district hospital were collecting parking fee from patients and their attendants for vehicles parked on the hospital premises, terming the same as illegal, arbitrary and contrary to the rules.Ambedkar urged the court to initiate action against the respondent authorities for allegedly collecting parking fee exceeding municipality rules under the Telangana Apartments Act 1987 and Telangana Municipalities Act and also in violation of a GO governing parking fee collection issued by the MA&UD department in Feb 2018, and in further violation of the Right to Health guaranteed by the Constitution.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Hyderabad | Silver Rate in Hyderabad | Bank Holidays in Hyderabad | Public Holidays in Hyderabad | Hyderabad AQI | Weather in Hyderabad | Petrol Price in Hyderabad | Diesel Price in Hyderabad | CNG Price in Hyderabad | LPG Price in HyderabadStay updated with the latest Hyderabad news. articles.title: Bihar hospital shocker: Masked man removes jewellery from dead body, calmly walks away
articles.summary: PATNA: A viral video from Siwan Model Sadar Hospital has raised serious questions over the security of patients and even bodies kept on the hospital
articles.body: PATNA: A viral video from Siwan Model Sadar Hospital has raised serious questions over the security of patients and even bodies kept on the hospital premises.The footage, reportedly from late Tuesday night, shows a masked man approaching a body lying near the registration counter and allegedly removing a chain from the deceased's neck before walking into the emergency ward without apparent obstruction.The authenticity of the video and the identity and role of the man have not yet been independently established. It is also unclear whether the deceased's family was aware of the removal of the chain or had given any consent.The video, however, has triggered questions over how an outsider was allegedly able to approach the body despite the presence of security personnel and CCTV surveillance at the hospital. Police verification of the footage and further investigation will be required to establish what exactly happened.According to hospital sources, the man seen in the video has been identified as Bablu Kumar. Sources claimed that he is frequently seen around the emergency ward at night.There are also allegations that he misleads patients arriving at the hospital into going to private nursing homes and operates a private ambulance. These allegations have not been independently verified.The latest incident has also brought back concerns over an earlier complaint involving the disappearance of jewellery from a deceased woman's body at the same hospital.A few days ago, relatives of a deceased woman had allegedly accused a female hospital sanitation worker of removing a silver anklet from the woman's foot. The woman was identified as Aarti Devi, 35, wife of Rajan Thakur of Bangra village under Maharajganj police station.Aarti had been referred to Siwan Sadar Hospital from Maharajganj Sub-Divisional Hospital after her condition deteriorated following a snakebite. She died while being brought to the Sadar Hospital. Her family later raised an allegation regarding the missing anklet. The sanitation worker was reportedly identified on the basis of CCTV footage and handed over to police.The latest viral video has once again put the hospital's security arrangements under scrutiny, particularly access to areas where bodies are kept before being handed over to relatives.Sadar hospital superintendent Dr Anil Kumar Singh said he was not aware of the latest incident.He said the CCTV footage would be examined on the basis of the viral video and that, if the person responsible is identified, the hospital would write to the local police station for appropriate legal action.The investigation is expected to establish whether the chain was actually removed from the deceased's body, who the person in the footage was and how he gained access to the area without intervention.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Patna | Silver Rate in Patna | Bank Holidays in Patna | Public Holidays in Patna | Patna AQI | Weather in Patna | Petrol Price in Patna | Diesel Price in Patna | CNG Price in Patna | LPG Price in PatnaStay updated with the latest Patna news. articles.title: MAHA loyalists accuse Trump administration of ‘broken promises’
articles.summary: Some supporters of the “Make America Healthy Again” movement have begun to publicly turn against Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and the Trump administration.
articles.body: Some supporters of the “Make America Healthy Again” movement have begun to publicly turn against their leader, Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., and the Trump administration as a whole as they demand tougher crackdowns on food dyes and pesticides. A scorecard released Thursday by MAHA activists, including former members of Kennedy’s 2024 presidential campaign, claims the Trump administration broke more than 85% of its promises to MAHA on food, agriculture and environmental health. The makers of the scorecard include Dave Murphy, a former fundraiser for Kennedy’s campaign, and Charles Eisenstein, Kennedy’s former chief speechwriter. NBC News is first to report on the scorecard, which offers a window into how MAHA views the administration, and Kennedy himself, ahead of the midterm elections. It accuses the Trump administration of doling out favors to the chemical industry, pointing to its decision to approve new pesticides and hire industry lobbyists and executives. “We’re asking the Trump administration to deliver on even the most basic promises they’ve made to the MAHA movement, and we’ve seen over and over again not just a lack of interest in doing so, but a blatant slap in the face,” said former Kennedy campaign adviser Tiffany Cianci, a MAHA advocate who authored the scorecard. About 41% of adults in the U.S. say they support MAHA ideals, according to an April poll from KFF, a nonprofit health think tank. Most are Republicans or Republican-leaning independents, according to the poll, though alignment with Kennedy or President Donald Trump wasn’t a primary reason for supporting the movement. MAHA coalesced during Kennedy’s presidential bid in 2024, then threw its support behind Trump when Kennedy endorsed him. It brought together multiple social movements, including food safety, environmentalism and vaccine skepticism, under the umbrella of taking on big corporations whose products may contribute to chronic diseases. But many of these advocates have become Kennedy’s harshest critics as of late, arguing that their priorities are being ignored by the Trump administration. Covid vaccine skeptics such as Dr. Mary Talley Bowden have criticized Kennedy and Trump for allowing mRNA vaccines to stay on the market. Food safety advocates say Kennedy hasn’t put enough pressure on companies to remove synthetic dyes and other additives from their products. And advocates for reducing pesticide exposure claim Trump undermined their mission by issuing an executive order to boost the supply of the weed killer glyphosate in the U.S. That dissatisfaction has led to infighting between Kennedy loyalists — including those appointed to key government positions — and activists faithful to their original cause. “What started out as a hairline crack in the coalition is now widened to be a gaping fissure,” said Peter Lurie, president of the Center for Science in the Public Interest, a nonprofit advocacy group focused on nutrition and food safety. White House spokeswoman Allison Schuster said the Trump administration “has already secured extensive victories for the MAHA Agenda, including overhauling the dietary guidelines for Americans, axing artificial ingredients in our food supply, and investing in regenerative farming.” “After years of being on the political sidelines, the MAHA coalition has found a champion in President Trump, who has made incredible strides to Make America Healthy Again,” Schuster said in a statement. Emily Hilliard, a spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services, said Kennedy “remains focused on delivering lasting reforms grounded in science, transparency, and accountability.” “President Trump and Secretary Kennedy are delivering the fundamental change Americans voted for. In just 20 months, this Administration has moved at a historic pace to advance MAHA across the federal government,” she said in a statement. Cianci acknowledged that many of the administration’s actions on environmental toxins and food additives have been outside of Kennedy’s purview. But his time in the administration has done “obvious harm” to his reputation, she said, noting that Kennedy’s career history involved suing the very pharmaceutical and pesticide companies the administration is now working with. “To see him not speaking out on the issues that are so obviously against everything that was promised is very hard because I believe ethically it’s probably working against his own inclinations,” Cianci said. Kelly Ryerson, a well-known MAHA advocate who goes by the moniker “Glyphosate Girl” and helped develop the scorecard, said she doesn’t fault Kennedy as much as the rest of Trump’s Cabinet because she knows “where his heart lies.” “I know how deep the forces are in terms of corporate influence on regulators, and it’s something that he himself has criticized for years,” she said. “[But] the actions of the administration have worked really in opposition to everything that we hoped and everything that Trump promised.” Pamela Herd, a professor of social policy at the University of Michigan, said the MAHA movement was always vulnerable to conflict because it consists of unusual bedfellows: liberal moms who feed their kids organic produce, fringe doctors who falsely claim that vaccines cause autism and Trump supporters who want to remove corporate influence from the federal government. Over time, though, MAHA’s main goals have solidified. A March poll from Politico suggests that removing ultra-processed foods from American diets and limiting exposure to PFAS, microplastics and pesticides were key priorities for people who self-identified as part of the movement. “What the MAHA movement has always been especially interested in is chemicals,” Lurie said. Much of Cianci’s scorecard focuses on actions taken by the Environmental Protection Agency and Agriculture Department — agencies Kennedy does not oversee. For instance, it considers the EPA’s decisions to weaken mercury emissions standards and roll back drinking water limits for certain PFAS as broken promises. Phasing out food dyes Several of the promises that were “partially kept,” according to the scorecard, come directly from Kennedy-led agencies like the Food and Drug Administration. For instance, the FDA asked food companies to voluntarily phase out certain dyes and banned two others that were not widely used. It also proposed a requirement for food manufacturers to notify the FDA when they determine that an additive is “generally recognized as safe.” The rule would not remove the additives already in food or prevent manufacturers from adding more, however. Lurie said Kennedy campaigned on fixing these issues, but “never took into account the practical aspects on the ground: What do the regulations actually look like? What authority do these agencies actually have?” The scorecard does not mention an action Kennedy has touted often: his January overhaul of the federal dietary guidelines, which encourages Americans to eat more protein and cut out ultra-processed foods. It also does not address Kennedy’s vaccination policies. Both Kennedy and Trump have attempted to reduce the number of universally recommended vaccines for children. And Kennedy last year fired the longtime members of a federal vaccine advisory committee, replacing them with vaccine skeptics. (A federal judge temporarily blocked the change, which is still being challenged in court.) “If you’re going to pick one thing that RFK was successful at, it’s very much how he has influenced government policy on vaccines,” Herd, the University of Michigan professor, said. Kennedy reassured anti-vaccine activists last month that they have “a strong and steadfast friend at the White House.” But as tensions mount, many MAHA supporters insist the movement does not need a political affiliation. Ryerson said MAHA voters will likely sit out the upcoming midterm elections. “The disappointments with Obama and Biden are similar to the disappointments with Trump,” she said. “The difference with this administration is that we are promised something very, very different in a very real way, so I think that that burn feels especially raw.”

articles.title: I’ve Treated Breast Cancer for 25 Years. Here’s What I Learned From My Own Diagnosis
articles.summary: For more than 20 years, Dr. Jennifer Litton has been treating breast cancer. Getting diagnosed with breast cancer herself showed her how far treatment has come.
articles.body: For more than 20 years, Dr. Jennifer Litton has been treating patients with breast cancer, particularly aggressive cases in young people and pregnant people. But her own family had been cancer-free until just a few years ago, Litton, 56, professor of breast medical oncology and chief clinical research officer at the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center, tells TODAY.com. She’d found herself in the “sandwich years,” she says, raising her three children, as well as caregiving for her parents (both of whom are now cancer patients), on top of a high-stress job. It’s at times like that when “we as women tend to not take care of ourselves,” Litton says. She’d started stress eating and stopped exercising as much. After her parents remarked that she “looked awful” — something “only your parents can say to you,” Litton says — she took stock of the changes in her life. Last fall, Litton decided to get all of her medical appointments taken care of, including getting her cholesterol checked, her colon cancer screening done and her mammogram. “I’ve been called back for mammograms all the time. I’ve had maybe three or four biopsies in the past,” she says. So, when she got the call to come back this time, she didn’t think much of it. But this time something was different. She looked at the images herself and saw “a whole big cluster of new calcifications,” she says, which are calcium deposits that form in breast tissue. While they’re often totally harmless, they can sometimes indicate a more serious issue, including breast cancer. “As I looked on (the screen), I was like, oh, that’s going to be something,” Litton recalls. ‘That’s Going to Be Something’ Litton had to do “what we ask all our patients to do,” she says. “In the middle of their life, of working, of taking care of their kids ... I was trying to fit in a diagnostic mammogram, an ultrasound. I had to fit all this into my busy life and navigate the healthcare system.” A biopsy ultimately revealed that Litton had ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS), a non-aggressive form of breast cancer sometimes called “Stage 0.” She describes the outer wall of the milk duct like a sausage casing “that’s thin but strong, and it keeps everything in the shape it’s supposed to be.” In DCIS, the cells are abnormal and dividing in an uncontrolled way, but are still contained within the sausage casing. “But you can imagine, as those cells divide, eventually they’re going to bust out and invade into the surrounding tissue,” she says, which is why it’s important to treat DCIS early. The diagnosis wasn’t a surprise for her. An estimated one in eight women will develop breast cancer in their lifetime, she says, adding, “There’s more than eight of us who take care of breast cancer patients at MD Anderson.” But for Litton, who typically spends her days treating patients with some of the most challenging, aggressive breast cancer cases, “I was always expecting the other shoe to drop,” she says. “At every step I was expecting I’m going to have to do a more aggressive surgery or radiation, or I’m certain to need chemo down the road,” she says. “And actually, I didn’t.” Surprisingly Less Invasive Treatment Although she’d briefly considered a double mastectomy to prevent the cancer from returning, Litton opted for a lumpectomy instead. This less invasive type of surgery involves removing only the tumor and a small area of healthy breast tissue surrounding it. Although she had to have a larger area removed than initially expected, she was able to have the plastic surgery team come at the same time. They made the area “look nicer than I think it would have if you left a 3 centimeter cavity there,” she laughs. After she healed, she underwent radiation treatments. Going through the process firsthand gave her a new perspective on the ways it’s changed during her career. For example, she was able to have targeted radiation, which didn’t involve the whole breast or lymph nodes, and meant she didn’t need tattoos to guide the radiation like she might have in the past. The hardest part for her was having to hold her arm up during the MRIs and radiation sessions. “I wasn’t expecting how much you have to get that arm ready and to be able to lift it up and keep it steady for a long period of time,” she says, adding that it’s now something she tells patients to be prepared for. The ‘True Beneficiary’ of Clinical Trials Being diagnosed with DCIS, “I know that I pulled the lucky straw out of breast cancer,” Litton says. But she also sees herself as the “true beneficiary of all the women who’ve been in all the clinical trials before,” she says. Her cancer was caught in the earliest possible stage through routine screening, and at every decision point during her cancer journey “I had solid, emerging data that I could take a turn for a less toxic intervention,” Litton says. For example, when deciding on surgery, radiation and a daily hormone medication, she was able to choose a less intense or invasive, tailor-made option for each than she could have even just five or 10 years ago. Insights Into the Emotional Side of a Cancer Journey The experience gave Litton a new window into the complex emotions that many cancer patients go through during and after treatment. First, she encountered the challenge of telling those around her about her diagnosis. And, outside of a few “medical girlfriends” and her family, she kept the situation private. “It wasn’t that I was trying to be secretive,” she explains. “It was just that, when I did tell a few people that weren’t in (the medical field), I had to stop and spend a lot of time consoling them and trying to explain.” It was something she just didn’t have the energy for on top of everything else, she realized, which came as a surprise. But, when she reached the end of her treatment and was getting ready to ring the bell at MD Anderson, “I said, You know, let’s just tell everyone,” she recalls, “and I didn’t really recognize how important that was.” She rang the bell surrounded by her family, colleagues and patient advocates. And now she brings up her personal experience when it helps patients who are anxious about part of treatment, for example, or navigating the next phase of life after a whirlwind of treatments and appointments. “You still don’t feel (normal), but you look OK, so all your friends are like, ‘Oh, she’s fine. She’s done chemo,’” Litton says. “And you have a moment to take a breath, and you’re like, what just happened to me?” Feelings like this, which Litton likens to “a kind of PTSD,” are something the medical world doesn’t talk about or ask patients about enough, she says. The same goes for young patients suddenly thrust into early menopause due to treatment, she says or those dealing with side effects from preventive hormone medications they need to keep taking even after they’re declared cancer-free. Rethinking What Wellness Looks Like After her diagnosis and treatment, Litton is approaching her wellness routine in a new way. She’s taking a medication called tamoxifen, a type of hormone therapy, which helps prevent another breast cancer from popping up. Litton has some of the usual side effects from the medication — “hot flashes, I’m a little crazier than I used to be, a little sweatier,” she says — but it’s another thing she’s able to bond with her patients over. And her relationships with exercise and food have evolved, too. “I got rid of the notion of, if I can’t do a full hour of exercise, I’m not really doing anything,” she says. “Anything you do is better than nothing,” she says. “If I can do five minutes, I should do five minutes.” Now, she does short bursts of activity throughout the day when she has time and keeps weights on her desk. When it comes to food, “I have the palate of an 11-year-old boy,” Litton laughs. Alongside her DCIS diagnosis, her heart scan “was also not very happy,” she says. So she’s gone from eating foods like cheeseburgers frequently to cutting out red meat and generally trying to eat unprocessed, whole foods. Of course, Litton will continue to get breast cancer screenings and be on the lookout for any changes in her body. “I feel like I’m doing everything I can,” she says. “I’m in a much healthier, stronger place than I was last year.”

articles.title: Grandmother of 12 holds plank for 5 hours in record-breaking feat
articles.summary: DonnaJean Wilde held an abdominal plank for five hours at the Huntsman World Senior Games, smashing her own Guinness world record by nearly 30 minutes.
articles.body: A 61-year-old Canadian grandmother broke the female abdominal plank world record after holding the position for five hours. DonnaJean Wilde accomplished the feat at the Huntsman World Senior Games in Utah on Oct. 4, breaking her own record by nearly 30 minutes, Storyful reported. Wilde’s plank began at 3:03 p.m. and ended at 8:03 p.m., with several judges rotating in and out of shifts during that period, a spokesperson for the World Senior Games told Storyful. FITNESS INFLUENCER SAYS ONE SIMPLE HABIT CAN HELP ANYONE GET BACK IN SHAPE Her previous record of 4 hours, 30 minutes and 11 seconds was set on March 21, 2004, at the Canadian high school where she once served as vice principal, according to the Guinness Book of World Records. "To successfully achieve the record, the challenger’s forearms and toes must touch the ground at all times," Guinness states. "The remainder of the body must be lifted off the ground and be kept straight throughout," it also says. FITNESS EXPERT REVEALS 6 THINGS PEOPLE OVER 35 SHOULD DO AFTER WORKOUTS TO STAY STRONG "My elbows hurt pretty bad," Wilde said after completing the previous record. "I was so worried about losing my form, and I think that’s why my quads hurt because I was just really tense." She shared with Guinness that the first two hours "went by quickly," but the next two hours were much more difficult. "The last hour was the most challenging, just to stay focused and keep my form," she said. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER During the last 30 minutes, she said she focused on "breathing, staying calm and not shaking." CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES Wilde first added planking to her daily routine years ago after breaking her wrist because she could perform the exercise while wearing a cast. "I realized that I could read and do things when I was planking and fell in love with it," she said, according to the report. Wilde shared some advice for others aiming to hold extended planks. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "Keep trying and keep practicing. When you have to read or work on your computer, just get on the floor and do it on the floor." Wilde has 12 grandchildren, according to Guinness. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Her new record is pending review and approval by Guinness.

articles.title: Parkinson's patients may protect memory and movement with one simple habit
articles.summary: A University of Cincinnati study links weekly physical activity to slower cognitive decline and motor function loss in Parkinson's disease patients.
articles.body: Weekly physical activity could help to slow down disease progression in Parkinson’s patients, a new study found. The research, led by the University of Cincinnati, included 294 patients with mild-to-moderate Parkinson's disease. Their average age was 66. The participants reported their weekly physical activity via questionnaires. ALAN ALDA REVEALS UNEXPECTED WEAPON IN HIS BATTLE AGAINST PARKINSON'S DISEASE Physical activity was assessed through structured interviews covering moderate and vigorous activities at work, at home and during recreation. Examples of moderate activity included brisk walking, light swimming, doubles tennis and household activities such as washing windows, vacuuming or mowing the lawn, the study release stated. Vigorous activity included pursuits like jogging, fast bicycling, team sports and singles tennis, along with shoveling and carrying heavy loads. Participants were divided into three groups based on their amount of weekly physical activity — up to four hours, four to eight hours and more than eight hours. PARKINSON'S IS BECOMING MORE COMMON; HERE ARE 5 THINGS EVERYONE SHOULD KNOW The researchers then monitored the participants’ cognitive health for up to five years and their motor function for up to seven years. Each additional hour of physical activity per week was linked to slightly slower declines in memory, thinking and movement abilities over time, even after accounting for factors such as age, sex, education, weight and disease severity. Patients who were physically active for four to eight hours per week experienced slower declines in memory and thinking abilities than those who exercised less than four hours. Exercise duration above eight hours per week did not appear to provide additional benefits for memory and thinking. The study was published Oct. 7 in Neurology, the official medical journal of the American Academy of Neurology. PARKINSON’S PATIENT’S YEARSLONG TREMOR VANISHES WITHIN MINUTES OF NEW ULTRASOUND TREATMENT "Parkinson’s disease is a brain disorder that causes movement and cognitive problems that gradually worsen, leading to disability and a loss of independence," study author Dong-Woo Ryu, M.D., Ph.D., of the University of Cincinnati and The Catholic University of Korea, said in the press release. "Previous research has shown associations between physical activity and movement symptoms. Our study found physical activity may have dual benefits, with associations with slower declines in movement and cognition." "While our study found small differences between activity levels, these differences may become more meaningful over time." Ryu pointed out that the potential benefits of physical activity for Parkinson’s patients may depend on how long they stay active and whether they continue exercising over time. "While our study found small differences between activity levels, these differences may become more meaningful over time," he said. The researchers cautioned that most participants had relatively strong thinking and memory skills when the study began, so additional research is needed to confirm the findings. "Exercise has well-established benefits for physical fitness and mobility, along with potential benefits for brain health through mechanisms that are not yet fully understood," Dr. Vibhash Sharma, a neurologist at UT Southwestern in Dallas, Texas, who specializes in Parkinson’s disease and other movement disorders, told Fox News Digital. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES "These findings further emphasize the importance of regular physical activity in managing Parkinson’s disease." One of the strengths of the study is that patients were followed over several years, with assessments of both motor and cognitive function, noted Sharma, who was not involved in the research. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER The study did have some limitations, the researchers acknowledged. Because the study was observational, it could not establish whether exercise directly slows Parkinson's disease progression. Also, as participants reported their own physical activity, they may not have accurately remembered how much they exercised. The participants were all located at a single location and were primarily White, which could limit the generalizability of the results, the researchers noted. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "It is also possible that patients with inherently slower-progressing disease are more likely to remain physically active," Sharma added. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Randomized studies are needed to confirm whether exercise directly slows cognitive or motor decline, according to the researchers. The study was supported by a grant from the Gardner Family Foundation and the Precision Medicine in Neurodegenerative Diseases Fund.
